result.reason: The passage is precisely the Gemara's opening 'michti' question — why does Shevuot follow Makkot — and its answer via the 'one prohibition liable for two punishments' link, which is exactly what the 'Michti Question' section prose describes.

The passage asks exactly the question described in the 'Full List in Shevuot' prose — why does Shevuot teach all of the two-which-is-four sets while Shabbat and Negaim present only their relevant portion — making the current placement correct.

The passage explains that oaths and tumah awareness are written together in the Torah and are similar in sharing a sliding-scale offering — this matches heading 0's prose about Torah juxtaposition, while the final clause 've-aydi de-tani tarti tani kulhu' is a secondary addendum that follows naturally from that explanation.

The passage directly addresses why Shevuot opens with oaths but first covers the shorter tumat mikdash material before returning to oaths, which is precisely what the 'Short Material First' section's prose describes.

All three items are consecutive mishna entries in the 'two which are four' list, and heading 8's prose explicitly introduces 'the full list of two-which-is-four cases,' making it the best fit for the entire passage including the oaths and tumah items that precede the Shabbat carrying discussion.

The passage explicitly discusses mara'ot nega'im (shades of leprous marks), se'et and baheret and their toldot, which matches exactly the 'Leprosy Types' section prose where the current placement already sits.

The passage is the Gemara's question about who authored the mishna and the two-part refutation of both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, which directly corresponds to the 'Authorship Question' section's prose about asking 'mani masnisin' and answering 'neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva'.

Both items — the gemara's suggestion that the mishnah can fit Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva via 'mehem le-chiyuv u-mehem le-patur,' and the immediate challenge to that reading — are precisely the content described in the 'Partial Application' prose, which explicitly discusses this approach and its rejection.

Both items are part of the same dialectical exchange about whether the mishnah's 'two-which-is-four' refers to korban liability or lashes, which is precisely what the 'Lashes Interpretation' prose describes — item 1 is an objection (the leprous marks comparison implies korban liability) and item 2 is the resolution (Rabbi Yishmael's view applies to korban, but lashes still apply for past oaths).

The passage is Rava's statement itself, which the 'Past Oaths & Lashes' section explicitly anticipates ('the gemara will elaborate this through Rava's comparison'), while the current heading 'Rava's Comparison' contains the essay author's extended prose explanation of what Rava means — the actual Talmudic quote belongs under the introductory heading that sets it up, not under the heading that analyzes it.

All six items form a continuous chain addressing the problem of lashes for a passive transgression (lav she-ein bo ma'aseh): the Gemara raises the difficulty, resolves it via Rabbi Yishmael's view, then challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan's consistency, cites his ruling of no-lashes for the 'will eat' case, and resolves the contradiction — exactly what candidate 5 ('Passive Transgression') describes as its topic.

All four items together form the gemara's challenge to using the notar mishna as support for Rabbi Yochanan — first identifying the candidate mishna, then explaining why it might support him, then questioning whether it follows Rabbi Yaakov or Rabbi Yehuda, then citing the baraita with both opinions — which precisely matches heading 7's prose about Rabbi Yehuda's reason and the lav ha-nitak le-asei challenge.
Both items together present the exact mishnah about two oaths on the same loaf resulting in only one liability, which is precisely what candidate 2 ('Two Oaths Mishnah') describes in its prose.

The passage directly presents the Gemara's inference from 'zo hi' that passive non-performance (said I will eat but did not) does not generate lashes, which is exactly what the prose under 'Active Violation Only' describes.

Both items present the Gemara's challenge about how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could have compiled two contradictory unattributed mishnayot, which is precisely what heading 0 ('Rabbi's Contradiction') discusses.

The passage summarizes the entire resolution — initial ruling, retraction, and the principle that a mishna does not move — which is best captured by the 'Summary & Resolution' section that synthesizes all these elements together, even though individual components appear in earlier sections.
